about: Sources for docs/research/toronto-accent/STUDY.md. Collected 2026-11-15 by Devin research sessions. 'what_it_shows' and 'notes' are the collector's own summary; anything marked UNVERIFIED was not confirmed. Video entries were reviewed through metadata, captions and (where possible) playback; no video was downloaded. Instagram entries come from hashtag-page captions only and are UNVERIFIED.

sources.title: Do You Know Toronto Slang?
sources.creator: Scott Anderson, U of T Magazine
sources.what_it_shows: Profile of Derek Denis's MTE research. Documents mans used as first-person pronoun ('Mans has work in the morning'), earliest UD attestation 'manz' 2006, Twitter 2010; mini-glossary: mans=I/we/them; ting=thing/casual relationship; ahlie=confirmational 'right?'; wallahi='I swear' from Somali (via Arabic); bucktee=pejorative from Somali for drug addict; nize it=shut up (clipping of 'recognize'). Drake's SNL 'Black Jeopardy' line 'I couldn't take the TTC but mans made it over anyway.'
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Reliable: university magazine interviewing the lead researcher.

sources.title: Why are wasteyutes a ting?
sources.creator: Bigelow, Gadanidis, Schlegl, Umbal & Denis (UPenn Working Papers in Linguistics)
sources.what_it_shows: Study of TH/DH-stopping in MTE: ~10% overall stopping rate in interviews, led by teenage males. Argues ting, wasteyute, mandem are enregistered spellings of a general stopping pattern tied to the stereotyped persona (young, male, suburban, nonwhite, low status).
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Peer-reviewed working paper; core phonology evidence.

sources.title: Toronto slang (Multicultural Toronto English)
sources.creator: Wikipedia
sources.what_it_shows: Overview of MTE: multi-ethnic dialect of young working-class racialized GTA speakers; sources Jamaican Patois, Arabic, Somali, AAVE; Jane-Finch founder effect (Baxter & Peters); Denis on outsized Somali influence via Rexdale; phonology: rhoticity, Low Back Merger Shift, GOOSE fronting, weaker Canadian raising, unraised pre-nasal TRAP, monophthongal GOAT, variable TH-stopping; long glossary incl. bare, cheesed, greezy, marved, miskeen, peng, wasteman, ahlie, dun know, gyaldem.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Wiki; good aggregator citing Denis, Bigelow et al.; verify against primary sources.

sources.title: Canadian raising
sources.creator: Wikipedia
sources.what_it_shows: /aI/ and /aU/ raise to mid onsets before voiceless consonants (price, clout) but not voiced (prize, cloud); about~[schwa-bUHt] stereotyped as 'aboot'; writer/rider distinguished by vowel after flapping; raised /aU/ fronter in central/eastern Ontario [EU~3U]; originated late 19th c.; references Chambers 1973, Boberg 2004/2008.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Solid summary with key citations.

sources.title: The History of Toronto Slang: Where It Came From & How It Developed
sources.creator: Toronto Mans Dictionary
sources.what_it_shows: Neighborhood account: slang built in inner suburbs Jane-Finch, Rexdale, Malvern/Scarborough; Jamaican immigration 60s-80s as biggest source (mans, man dem, wagwan, ahlie, bare); Somali refugee wave early 90s layered wallahi etc.; Jimmy Prime credited with 'the 6ix' before Drake's Views; cites Walrus and Globe pieces on commodification debates.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Community dictionary site, cites Denis's work; medium reliability.

sources.title: Canadian raising and other oddities
sources.creator: York University linguistics page (Taylor Roberts)
sources.what_it_shows: Clear explanation: /ay/ and /aw/ raise to mid vowels before voiceless obstruents /p,t,k,s,f/; 'aboot' is a mishearing (vowel raises to mid, not high /u/); notes Torontonians' unique pronunciation of the city's name.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. University linguistics teaching page with audio examples.

sources.title: Appendix: Glossary of Canadian English
sources.creator: Wiktionary contributors
sources.what_it_shows: Definitions: double-double (coffee, two creams two sugars), toque (knitted hat), eh (tag for agreement/'huh?'), loonie/toonie, washroom, chesterfield, mickey, two-four, serviette, parkade, homo milk, Gostapo (GO Transit security).
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Crowdsourced but reasonable for vocabulary.

sources.title: A brief guide to Turrono slang
sources.creator: Gabrielle Warren, The Varsity (U of T student paper)
sources.what_it_shows: Early campus glossary: marved (hungry), styll (sentence-final emphasis/~'though': 'Mans out here are fine, styll'), wasteman/waste yute, cheesed, fam/fom, reach, sweetermans, ting, bare, gyaldem/mandem; notes origin in Scarborough.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. 2016 snapshot — useful for what was current then vs now.

sources.title: Toronto Slang: The Ultimate Guide For Everyday Situations
sources.creator: Eul Basa, Narcity
sources.what_it_shows: Glossary with example lines: ahlie ('right?'), are u dumb, bare ('Yo bare sweeties at Eaton'), come thru, cyattie, deafaz, differently, dun kno, fam/fom, from time, greezy, merked, link up, lowe, nize it, run up freak, snake, styll, two-twos, wagwan ('Wagwan my G?'), wasteman ('Bare wastemans tryna cop a fry from me tho'), waste yute, gyaldem/mandem, ting. Notes Scarborough-vs-west-end origin debate and Jamaican Patois roots.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Millennial-media listicle; definitions loosely sourced but widely consistent with academic sources.

sources.title: Here are the top 10 most mispronounced places in Toronto
sources.creator: Global News (reporting Preply list)
sources.what_it_shows: List: Toronto = 'tuh-ronno' not 'toe-ron-toe' ('pronouncing the second T sounds pretentious, a dead giveaway'); Geoffrey=jeh-free; Etobicoke=et-toh-bee-co (silent k, from Ojibwe 'wadoopikaang'); Yonge='young'; Wellesley=WELLZ-ly; Grosvenor=gro-vner.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. News coverage of a Preply listicle; place-name details consistent with other sources.

sources.title: A Dictionary of English in Multicultural Toronto
sources.creator: Melissa Douglas & Shiyan Liang, Canadian Language Museum (consultants Derek Denis, Vidhya Elango)
sources.what_it_shows: SSHRC-funded dictionary w/ song-lyric citations: aboki (Hausa), ahlie (Jamaican Patois 'right?'), bare, bredrin, bucktee (Somali: homeless/drug addict/loser), bumbaclot, cheesed, cop, cut, deep it, dukes (parents), dunno/'ya dun know' (Kardinal 'Bakardi Slang' 2000 'T-dot say's Yuh dun know'), from time, fam, man dem (Michie Mee 1991 lyric), mans (Mustafa 'Air Forces' 2021 lyric), marites (Tagalog), marved, mashallah/miskeen (Arabic), murked, nize it (Patois 'noise'), styll ('bout to reach K-BBQ styll'), ting (Sadboi 'X-Ting' lyric), T-dot, waste yute. Intro: 55.7% of Torontonians visible minorities (2021 census); Jamaican community greatest influence; Somali arrivals mostly 1991-2000.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. High-quality community dictionary, expert-reviewed; the single best slang glossary source.

sources.title: The Toronto Accent Is Real
sources.creator: Maia Wyman, The Walrus
sources.what_it_shows: Feature on MTE vs 'Normative Toronto English'; Denis on Jamaican Patwa as major influence, Somali (bucktee), Arabic (wallahi); accent belongs predominantly to Black community (Jamaican/Bajan immigrants from 1950s on); slang emerged late 90s-2000s; TikTok mockery and 'worst accent' discourse; commodification/appropriation debate incl. Ryan Persadie on Drake's 'embodied Caribbeanization'; code-switching and anti-Black stigma.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Longform journalism quoting Denis and scholars; strong on social context and stigma.

sources.title: Toronto slang on the rise thanks to city's growing pop culture relevance
sources.creator: Salmaan Farooqui, The Globe and Mail (Canadian Press)
sources.what_it_shows: Denis interviewed: slang demarcates in-crowd; 'Milwaukee Bucktees' sign during Raptors run (bucktee from Somali); nize it=shut up, waste yute=silly kid (Patois roots); wallahi=swear on God; ahlie 'functions similarly to eh in normative Canadian English'; Kardinal Offishall's BaKardi Slang (2000) as early lexicon reference; student shame around the variety.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Wire piece; the ahlie~eh functional parallel is a key insight.

sources.title: Sah-ry, eh? We're in the midst of the Canadian Vowel Shift
sources.creator: Maclean's magazine
sources.what_it_shows: Accessible account of Canadian Shift: 'God'->'gawd', 'pillow'->'pellow', 'Timbit'->'Tembet', 'Dan'->'Don', sorry less like 'sore-y'; discovered 1995 (Clarke et al.); suspected epicentre urban Ontario; young women leading; De Decker: vowels getting 'higher and backer' (re: back vowels).
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Journalism; good plain-language examples; direction of movement simplified.

sources.title: Linguistics professor uncovering Toronto's unique style of English
sources.creator: Ali Raza, U of T Mississauga via Phys.org
sources.what_it_shows: Denis on MTE findings (J Engl Ling 2023): 'I almost missed the TTC but mans made it here anyways'; Canadian raising avoided in 'about' (stereotype awareness) but present in 'ice' vs 'eyes'; GOAT monophthongization traced to Jamaican Patois; 'Tronno' vs 'Tor-on-toh' as authenticity marker; MTE as 'feature pool' not a dialect.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. University PR piece; direct quotes from Denis.

sources.title: The Social Meaning of Eh in Canadian English
sources.creator: Derek Denis (CLA 2013 proceedings)
sources.what_it_shows: History of eh: earliest attestation Goldsmith 1773 (British); Canadian attestation Haliburton's Clockmaker 1836; Avis's narrative/exclamative eh unique to Canada; tracks how eh became enregistered stereotype via indexical orders (Silverstein/Johnstone); commodification; mismatches between actual use and reported use.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Conference paper by the MTE lead scholar; excellent eh background.

sources.title: A note on mans in Toronto
sources.creator: Derek Denis, Toronto Working Papers in Linguistics
sources.what_it_shows: Core mans paper: plural noun 'mans' grammaticalizing into first-person singular pronoun in multiethnic adolescent Toronto English, parallel to man in Multicultural London English (Cheshire 2013) but with differences; raises questions of contact vs independent innovation via Jamaican Creole.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Primary scholarly source for mans.

sources.title: The top 10 most mispronounced places in Toronto, from Etobicoke to Queens Quay
sources.creator: CityNews Toronto
sources.what_it_shows: Same Preply list with all ten: Toronto 'Tuh-Ronno'; Geoffrey 'Jeh-Free'; Etobicoke 'Et-Toh-Bee-Co'; Yonge 'Young'; Wellesley 'Wellz-Ly'; Grosvenor 'Gro-Vner'; The Esplanade 'Esplan-Aad'; Strachan 'Strawn'; Spadina 'Spuh-Dee-Nah' (not 'Spuh-Die-Nah'); Roncesvalles 'Rawn-Ses-Vay-Yez'; adds Trethewey 'Treh-Thoo-Wee' (rank 26).
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Local news; street-name pronunciations broadly corroborated.

sources.title: Toronto Slang: Popular Words, Meanings, and Examples
sources.creator: Slangiify
sources.what_it_shows: Table glossary: mans (I/me/you/we/people, context-dependent), mandem (the guys), ting (can sound objectifying), bare ('not unique to Toronto'), marved, styll/'still' (final 'though'), deep it, wagwan ('what's going on?'), yallah/chalo (Arabic/South Asian 'let's go'), two-twos, mazza, leng, nize it, waste yute; notes Jamaican/Somali/Arabic/South Asian contributions and overlap with UK slang.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. SEO slang blog; medium-low reliability, useful cross-check only.

sources.title: 70+ Toronto Slang Words You Need to Know
sources.creator: wikiHow
sources.what_it_shows: Long glossary: aboki, ahlie, ballin' up, bare, blem, bredrin, cut, dun kno, fam, from time, gheez, GTA, link up, marved, merked, mickey, mossin', nize it, nyeah eh, reach, say less, styll, two-twos, wallahi, waste yute, the 6ix.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. General-audience guide; verify terms against academic/community sources.

sources.title: New research study will finally explain how people pronounce Toronto
sources.creator: Amy Carlberg, blogTO
sources.what_it_shows: On Caitlin Bergin's (Carleton) sociolinguistic survey of how Torontonians say 'Toronto' by GTA postal code and in/out-group; tote-bag spellings TERANO, TRAWNO, TRONNO, TARONNA, TORONOE; notes lively debate on the city's subreddit with hundreds of responses.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Good on variation as identity marker.

sources.title: 15 things you need to explain to first-time visitors to Toronto
sources.creator: Phoebe Knight, blogTO
sources.what_it_shows: Tourist-oriented: locals drop first 'o' and second 't' -> 'T'ronno'/'Tuhronno'/'Churonno'; Yonge='young', Strachan='strawn', Etobicoke='eh-toe-bi-coe', Tecumseth='teh-come-see'; nicknames (Hogtown, Big Smoke, T Dot, 6ix) rarely used in conversation; not everyone speaks with the viral 'Toronto accent'.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. City guide; reflects folk knowledge, consistent with academic description.

sources.title: The list of Toronto's top slang words may surprise you
sources.creator: blogTO staff (reporting Preply tweet analysis)
sources.what_it_shows: Preply analysis of ~130,000 geotagged tweets: Toronto's most-used slang word was 'dart' (cigarette), with 'mickey' and 'baby girl' also common; 'whose mans'/'waste yute' didn't make top cut — i.e., everyday Toronto slang skews more Letterkenny than Drake.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Secondhand report of a marketing-firm tweet scrape; weak methodology, interesting counterpoint.

sources.title: The third dialect of English: Some Canadian evidence
sources.creator: Sandra Clarke, Ford Elms, Amani Youssef — Language Variation and Change 7(2)
sources.what_it_shows: Founding Canadian Shift paper: lax vowels of Canadian English shifting, pivot argued to be the cot/caught low back merger; lowering/retraction of kit/bet/bat; conditioning by following consonant voicing/manner; gender differences; back vowel fronting.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Abstract page; the citation for 'Canadian Shift' itself.

sources.title: 'If ur from Toronto you'll understand': register change and metadiscursive engagement with mediatized Multicultural Toronto English
sources.creator: Derek Denis et al., English Language & Linguistics (2025)
sources.what_it_shows: Defines MTE as a register associated with racialized youth; enregisterment driven by social-media metadiscourse disseminating the register wider; audience recontextualization as engine of register change; defines multiethnolect as languaging practices of young people in urban working-class neighbourhoods of first arrival.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Abstract+intro of peer-reviewed article; best current framing of MTE-as-register.

sources.title: A Delightful Dictionary for Canadian English
sources.creator: The New Yorker
sources.what_it_shows: On DCHP-2 (2nd ed., 11 years at UBC under Stefan Dollinger): 'eh' entry ~5,000 words covering confirmational/contesting/pardon-eh/narrative uses (excluded from 1967 1st ed.); hoser coined by Moranis & Thomas on SCTV 1981; toque 'one of the most widely known Canadianisms' (spelling vs [u] pronunciation confuses non-Canadians); double-double & two-four as identity markers; chesterfield now moribund.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Reliable secondary account of the authoritative Canadianisms dictionary.

sources.title: Language Log: 'Say less'
sources.creator: Mark Liberman, Language Log
sources.what_it_shows: Documents spread of 'say less' as substitute for 'say no more' over ~a decade; UD entries back to 2011; 2018 Hypebeast interview with Roy Woods (album 'Say Less', 2017) attributes the expression to Toronto street slang.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Linguist-run blog; the Toronto attribution is via a music interview (moderate).

sources.title: Toronto slang: 15 words you'll hear in the 6ix, eh
sources.creator: Mark Wills, ProperSlang
sources.what_it_shows: Mixed Canadian+MTE guide: the 6ix (416/647 codes or 6 pre-amalgamation municipalities; older T-dot, Hogtown); mans ('Mans is tired'), ahlie (~Patois 'a lie?'), styll ('I'm not going, styll'), skeen (twist on Jamaican 'seen' = agreed/understood, can mean 'whatever' flatly), nize it, eh, toque, double-double, loonie, keener, give'r, gong show, chirp, deke.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Slang blog; includes a 'use them like a local' respect caveat; medium reliability.

sources.title: Toronto Mans Dictionary — Real Toronto Slang, Defined (73+ Words)
sources.creator: Toronto Mans Dictionary
sources.what_it_shows: Community dictionary with term+example+origin tags: 'llow it (let it go); 416 vs 905 identity codes; 6ix God (Drake's title); ahlie (Patois 'a lie'); bare; big up; blem; bless up; bredren; brodie/crodie; buff; certi; cheesed; chirping; endz ('your neighbourhood, home turf': 'Come through the endz this weekend'); fam; flex; for tru; greasy; GTA; gwap; gyal/gyaldem; Hogtown (19th c. political insult + meatpacking); hooooly; irie; Jane and Finch; leng; link up.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Community-run dictionary citing origins per term; medium-high for glosses/examples.

sources.title: Drake
sources.creator: The Canadian Encyclopedia
sources.what_it_shows: States 'the 6'/'the 6ix' was coined by rapper Jimmy Prime; refers to 416/647 area codes and/or six pre-amalgamation municipalities; announced via 'Views From the 6' title July 2014, worldwide Twitter trend; tracks incl. '6 God', '6 Man', 'You & the 6', 'Know Yourself' ('Runnin' through the 6 with my woes').
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Authoritative encyclopedia entry.

sources.title: Canadian English
sources.creator: Wikipedia
sources.what_it_shows: Standard Canadian English overview: French loans (poutine, toque), homegrown vocab (chesterfield, double-double), Low-Back-Merger Shift shared with western US since 1980s; lists 'Toronto' among named dialects; history of the field (Avis, Geikie 1857 'corrupt dialect' remark).
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. General reference.

sources.title: UTM linguistics professor uncovering Toronto's unique style of English
sources.creator: Ali Raza, University of Toronto Mississauga
sources.what_it_shows: Original UTM version of the phys.org piece: MTE named by Denis's team; mans-as-'I' example with TTC; Canadian raising avoided in stereotype-loaded 'about' but kept in ice/eyes; GOAT monophthongization linked to Jamaican Patois; 'Tronno' as community authenticity feature; feature-pool model.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. University newsroom; same content as phys.org, included as institutional corroboration.

sources.title: Taronna names: How our city leaves us tongue-tied
sources.creator: Curtis Rush, Toronto Star
sources.what_it_shows: On the TTC automated-announcer 'Spadina' debate: original 'Spa-deenah' vs popular 'Spa-Dinah' (long usage winning per the Star); Roncesvalles 'Rrrrrawn-ses-vay-yez' (or 'Roncy'); Princes' Gate not 'Princess'; Baby Point pronounced 'Bawby' (after settler James Baby); Yonge='Young Street', 'don't make it rhyme with sponge'.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Top local paper with historian Mike Filey; great for place-name nuances.

sources.title: 17 things you need to know if you're moving to Toronto for university
sources.creator: Ainsley Smith, Daily Hive
sources.what_it_shows: Tip #1: 'It's pronounced Tronno not Tor-on-Toe — no bigger way to scream you're not from here than overemphasizing the T's'; also 'Turrono' variant; calls Toronto 'the most linguistically diverse city in Canada' (~200 languages).
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. City-guide folk account; matches linguistic description.

sources.title: The cot-caught distinction in Canadian and American English
sources.creator: Rishi Gopinath, Our Languages blog (Language Portal of Canada, Govt of Canada)
sources.what_it_shows: Explains /ɑ/ vs /ɒ/: Canadians merge both to /ɒ/ (don=dawn, cot=caught, pond=pawned); Inland North US and NYC keep distinct; Californians merge to /ɑ/ — i.e. Canadians and Bostonians merge the OTHER way.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Government language blog by a GTA writer; clear minimal pairs.

sources.title: How Canadian was eh? A baseline investigation of usage and ideology
sources.creator: Canadian Journal of Linguistics (Derek Denis)
sources.what_it_shows: Eh as confirmational seeking addressee confirmation; in modern Toronto corpora eh is INFREQUENT vs other confirmationals yet remains 'the quintessential Canadian English stereotype'; investigates whether it was ever more frequent, comparing Southern Ontario and Vancouver Island corpora.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Abstract page of peer-reviewed article; key for 'real uses of eh today'.

sources.title: So different and pretty cool! Recycling intensifiers in Toronto, Canada
sources.creator: Sali A. Tagliamonte, English Language & Linguistics 12(2)
sources.what_it_shows: ~10,000 adjectival heads from Toronto interviews: 'very' rapidly declining, 'really' expanded dramatically, 'so' and 'pretty' rising; 36.1% of adjectives intensified; recycling model of intensifier renewal.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Abstract+details; classic Toronto variationist study.

sources.title: Language Log: Chranna and Fluffya
sources.creator: Mark Liberman, Language Log
sources.what_it_shows: NPR transcript: Torontonian physician says [ˈtɹɐɾ̃ə] with nasal tap, 'there's no t in it'; quotes Jack Chambers (U of T): locals drop the second t through sheer frequency of saying the name; Wikipedia variants 'Toronno, Trono, Toranna, Taranna, Chrono, Chranna, Terawhnna'; Ben Zimmer: 'Trawna' is the best pronunciation-spelling.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Linguist blog; nasal-flap detail is the phonetic mechanism behind 'Trawna'.

sources.title: Why not just anyone can use the Toronto accent for internet clout
sources.creator: CBC Arts Commotion (Sandy Hudson, Matt Amha, Radheyan Simonpillai)
sources.what_it_shows: Debate on who may profitably perform the Toronto accent; Sandy Hudson (grew up Jamaican-background North York/Scarborough): words she 'had to learn in the culture', notes code-switching necessity vs comedians using the accent as punchline.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Very recent; strong on appropriation/code-switching ethics.

sources.title: What can we tell from how someone speaks? (The Accent Effect)
sources.creator: Lakshine Sathiyanathan, Lisa Xing — CBC News
sources.what_it_shows: CBC Toronto series on accent attitudes: Jamaican-Canadian takeout owner in Scarborough code-switches into patois for customers ('He speaks patois!' vs Canadians 'you have a strong accent' — intelligibility and status perceptions).
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Reported feature; documents patois/English code-switching in Scarborough daily life.

sources.title: Exploring the Vowel Space of Multicultural Toronto English
sources.creator: Denis, Elango, Nor Kamal, Prashar & Velasco — Journal of English Linguistics
sources.what_it_shows: First systematic sociophonetic study of MTE (Brampton, GTA youth, 2018 fieldwork): tests GOOSE fronting, Canadian Shift, Canadian raising, ban/bag tensing, GOAT monophthongization; high interspeaker variability; young immigrant men least normative; MTE as variable repertoire/'linguistic alterity' and everyday resistance. Context: 46% of GTA population immigrants, 51% visible minority.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. The core MTE phonology paper.

sources.title: Fom and friends: Respellings, enregisterment, and variable pre-nasal /ae/ in Multicultural Toronto English
sources.creator: Vidhya Elango & Derek Denis (CLA 2021 proceedings)
sources.what_it_shows: Feature inventory of MTE: th-stopping, GOAT monophthongization, lack of MOUTH raising, ahlie (confirmational from Jamaican Patwa), styll (utterance-final concessive), pronominal mans (1sg or 3rd person), a/an allomorphy loss ('a apple', Schlegl & Tagliamonte 2021), lexical loans from Patwa and Somali specifically (the city's two largest Black racialized groups). Analyzes 'fom'/'fham' respelling of 'fam' as indexing laxer pre-nasal /ae/ (against NAm pre-nasal tensing, Boberg 2008/2010).
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Dense but the single best MTE feature inventory.

sources.title: Canadian Slang & Vocabulary: Essential English and French Terms
sources.creator: Berlitz Canada
sources.what_it_shows: Core Canadianisms with examples: eh ('right?'), toque, double-double ('I'll have a double-double and a Boston cream'), clicks (km), chesterfield (older), give 'er, two-four ('May two-four' weekend), Hollywood North; everyday terms table incl. washroom, hydro.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Language-school blog; reliable for standard vocabulary.

sources.title: 57 Canadian slang words you need to learn
sources.creator: Contiki
sources.what_it_shows: Travel-guide glossary of Canadianisms (toque, loonie/toonie, double-double, keener, give'r, stagette, pop, runners, mickey, two-four, hydro bill, parkade, dart).
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Travel brand; vocab corroboration only.

sources.title: 40 Things You'll Hear A Scarborough Person Say
sources.creator: Narcity
sources.what_it_shows: Older (2015) Scarborough-centric list: styll as synonym for 'though' at sentence end ('I've ate like 3 patties I needa go to the gym styll'); waste yute ('Stop mall ratting ya waste yute!!'); ting as Patois 'thing' + person you're casually seeing ('All the tings are at Caribana fom you down?').
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Dated in places — good baseline for dated-vs-current tracking.

sources.title: What's with the weird British pronunciation of words like Gloucester?
sources.creator: The Straight Dope
sources.what_it_shows: Notes Canadians routinely elide: 'When was the last time you heard a Canadian pronounce all three syllables, or the second t, in Toronto? It's Tronno, more like' — framed as ordinary speech-compression like placenames everywhere.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Q&A column; anecdotal but consistent.

sources.title: We The 6: Why the name Drake gave us is here to stay
sources.creator: The Globe and Mail
sources.what_it_shows: On the July 14 2014 'Views from the 6' announcement: initial Torontonian skepticism ('WE DONT CALL IT THE 6 BRO'), then adoption; 'Runnin' through the 6 with my woes' as singalong reference; name tied to area codes/six municipalities.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Contemporaneous 2015 report on the nickname's reception.

sources.title: The Lax Vowel Subsystem in Canadian English Revisited
sources.creator: Rebecca Roeder & Lidia-Gabriela Jarmasz, Toronto Working Papers in Linguistics 31
sources.what_it_shows: First wide-scale acoustic description of the Canadian Shift in mainstream Toronto English (35 natives from Tagliamonte's 2003-06 Toronto corpus, ~1800 tokens): front lax vowels retract AND lower together; retraction dominates recent change; little change since WWII era; argues redistribution in reconfigured space after low back merger rather than a pull-chain.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Working-paper version of their CJL 2010 article; key Toronto data.

sources.title: Atlas of North American English, Ch. 15: Canada
sources.creator: Labov, Ash & Boberg (ANAE)
sources.what_it_shows: Low back merger general across Canada; Scargill & Warkentyne 1972 survey of 14,000+ schoolchildren/parents: ~85% say cot/caught rhyme (true rate near 100%); Newfoundland exception ~70%; Don-dawn merger near-uniform before /n/; Chambers 1993 literary evidence of merger in Ontario speech mid-19th c., possibly from merged Pennsylvania Loyalist settlement.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Authoritative atlas chapter; best cot-caught numbers.

sources.title: TORONTO SLANG EXPLAINED! / Translated
sources.creator: Toronto Streets Magazine
sources.what_it_shows: Glossary: mans (group of people or 'I/me', Caribbean influence); ting (girl/thing/event, Jamaican Patois); waste yute/wasteman (useless person; yute<youth); fam (close friends); frames slang as product of 'the 6ix' multiculturalism.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Local culture magazine; medium reliability.

sources.title: Toronto's Slang Isn't 'New.' It's Black
sources.creator: Sharine Taylor, VICE
sources.what_it_shows: Essential critique: ting, man dem, waste yute, wallahi, bucktee are from Toronto's Black diasporic communities (Caribbean + East African); ting/man dem from Jamaican Patois, bucktee Somali; calls out mainstream coverage (Vanity Fair/Lilly Singh, CP piece, CityNews segment) for erasing Black speakers; analogy to AAVE and code-switching consequences.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Opinion/analysis; crucial for respectful framing and crediting communities.

sources.title: The Role of Social Factors in the Canadian Vowel Shift: Evidence from Toronto
sources.creator: Michol F. Hoffman — American Speech 85(2)
sources.what_it_shows: Acoustic study of bit/bet/bat in Toronto interviews across British, Italian, Chinese ancestry groups: age and sex matter but NO significant ethnicity differences for vowel height/backness — all Toronto ethnic groups participate in the shift.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Abstract page (PDF paywalled); key point that mainstream shift is pan-ethnic in Toronto.

sources.title: Vowel production in Winnipeg
sources.creator: Robert Hagiwara, University of Manitoba (CJL)
sources.what_it_shows: Acoustic study (10 Winnipeg natives, /hVd/+/hVt/ word list): confirms low-back merger, /ae/ retraction, /u,ʊ/ advancement; finds Canadian raising is a shift of BOTH nucleus and offglide across /aɪ,aʊ,oɪ/, not just nucleus heightening; questions uniformity of 'Canadian Shift' vs California.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Full working PDF; useful phonetic detail on raising mechanics.

sources.title: [d]at's loud, bro! A report on TH-stopping in Multicultural Toronto English
sources.creator: Bigelow, Gadanidis, Schlegl, Umbal & Denis (Buffalo-Toronto workshop slides, 2019)
sources.what_it_shows: Slides summarizing MTE feature list: lexical ((waste)yute, ting, mandem, cheesed, cut, deafaz, nize your beak, wallahi, bare), discourse-pragmatic (ahlie confirmational, styll concessive), morphosyntax (pronominal mans), phonology (Canadian Shift, GOOSE fronting participation; variation in Canadian raising, no short-a nasal split, GOAT monophthongization); TH/DH-stopping ~10%, led by males; enregisterment via orthographic ting/yute/dem.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Conference slides by the research team; compact feature inventory.

sources.title: Canadian Raising: Retrospect and Prospect
sources.creator: J.K. Chambers — Canadian Journal of Linguistics
sources.what_it_shows: Retrospective by the phenomenon's namer: documentary evidence to 1934, comparative atlas data pushes origin to late 19th century; US northern /aɪ/ raising is a different (overlapping) phenomenon; possible threat to /aʊ/ raising from aw-fronting turned out accidental.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Abstract page; authority on chronology of the feature.

sources.title: Deconstructing variation in pragmatic function: A transdisciplinary case study
sources.creator: Denis et al. — Language in Society
sources.what_it_shows: Case study of pragmatic markers (confirmational system incl. eh and related forms in Toronto data) using transdisciplinary methods; relevant to how 'eh' and discourse tags vary by function rather than being interchangeable.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Abstract page; supports eh/ahlie function comparison.

sources.title: Multicultural London English
sources.creator: Wikipedia
sources.what_it_shows: The comparison variety: MLE arose in dense immigrant London neighbourhoods; features include man-as-pronoun (Cheshire 2013), TH-stopping/fronting, monophthongal GOAT, 'innit' confirmational, syllable-timed rhythm — the template Denis models MTE on; explains independent-but-parallel mans/man development debate.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. Background for why Toronto~London words overlap (shared Jamaican diaspora).

sources.title: The Canadian Shift in Toronto
sources.creator: Rebecca V. Roeder & Lidia-Gabriela Jarmasz — CJL 55(3)
sources.what_it_shows: Published version: for ~70 years the shift has NOT affected high front lax /i/; (ɛ) and (æ) lower and retract, retraction now dominant and slowing; continued retraction of the merged low-back vowel implicated; proposes parallel shift (Vowel Dispersion Theory), not a chain shift.
sources.notes: read 2026-11-15. DOI/abstract page; definitive mainstream Toronto findings.
